Both disclosures concern the U.S. regulatory capital framework for Goldman Sachs and GS Bank USA as Category I/Advanced approach banking organizations. D074 establishes their Category I status and Advanced approach designation under the Capital Framework (Basel III/Dodd-Frank). D083 details the specific implementation of these standards, including the calculation of risk-based capital ratios under Standardized and Advanced Capital Rules and the associated conservation buffers. They share the same specific subject of the entity's capital requirement regime.

previous_disclosures.summary: GS and GS Bank USA are subject to Category I standards as a global systemically important bank, requiring compliance with Advanced approach capital and liquidity measures under the FRB's Capital Framework, which implements Basel III and Dodd-Frank provisions, with capital sufficiency subject to qualitative regulatory judgments.

current_disclosures.section: Regulation > Banking Supervision and Regulation > THE GOLDMAN SACHS GROUP, INC. AND SUBSIDIARIES
current_disclosures.summary: Goldman Sachs calculates risk-based capital ratios under Standardized and Advanced Capital Rules, which include minimum requirements and additional conservation buffers composed primarily of Common Equity Tier 1 capital; failure to meet these constraints capital distributions and compensation. The stress capital buffer (SCB) reflects stressed losses from CCAR, includes planned dividends, and has a 2.5% floor, with the FRB approving capital distributions if a BHC must resubmit its capital plan.

The addition of SCB detail is clarifying existing capital requirements rather than introducing a new material risk or changing the strategic position. It is a routine disclosure update on regulatory mechanics.

comparisons.peer_summary: Bank of America is subject to an extensive U.S. federal regulatory framework primarily for the protection of depositors and the Deposit Insurance Fund, with supervision by the Federal Reserve for the holding company and banks, and by the OCC, FDIC, and Federal Reserve for its U.S. bank subsidiaries.
comparisons.comparison: While both GS and Bank of America are subject to U.S. federal regulatory frameworks and capital requirements, the target disclosure for GS focuses specifically on the mechanics of the Capital Framework (Basel III, G-SIB Category I status, quantitative measures), whereas Bank of America's cited disclosure focuses on the broader purpose of the regulatory framework (protection of depositors and the DIF) and the supervisory bodies (Federal Reserve, OCC, FDIC).

sentences.text: The Capital Framework is largely based on the Basel Committee's framework for strengthening the regulation, supervision and risk management of banks (Basel III) and also implements certain provisions of the Dodd-Frank Act.
Under the Capital Framework, we and GS Bank USA must meet specific regulatory capital requirements that involve quantitative measures of assets, liabilities and certain off-balance sheet items.

U.S. federal regulation of banks, BHCs and financial holding companies is intended primarily for the protection of depositors and the Deposit Insurance Fund (DIF) rather than for the protection of shareholders and creditors.

Our U.S. bank subsidiaries (the Banks), organized as national banking associations, are subject to regulation, supervision and examination by the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC), the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) and the Federal Reserve.

comparisons.peer_topic: Regulatory Capital Treatment of Deferred Tax Assets
comparisons.peer_summary: Of the $29.8 billion in net DTAs, $12.8 billion was deducted from regulatory capital (primarily tax carry-forwards), while the remaining $17.0 billion was not deducted and was appropriately risk-weighted under Basel III standards.
comparisons.comparison: Both disclosures concern regulatory capital calculations, but they address different components. GS describes the overall framework (Basel III, G-SIB) and the requirement to meet specific quantitative measures for assets and liabilities. Citi's disclosure details the specific treatment of Deferred Tax Assets (DTAs) within that regulatory capital calculation, noting that $12.8 billion was deducted. This represents a specific accounting detail within the broader framework described by GS.

sentences.text: Under the Capital Framework, we and GS Bank USA must meet specific regulatory capital requirements that involve quantitative measures of assets, liabilities and certain off-balance sheet items.
Of Citi's total net DTAs of $29.8 billion as of December 31, 2024, $12.8 billion, primarily related to tax carry-forwards, was deducted in calculating Citi's regulatory capital.

The remaining $17.0 billion of net DTAs as of December 31, 2024 was not deducted in calculating regulatory capital pursuant to Basel III standards and was appropriately risk weighted under those rules.

comparisons.peer_summary: The Federal Reserve and OCC establish capital and liquidity requirements consistent with Basel III, with ongoing global refinements and U.S. proposals to revise risk-based capital requirements for large banks; finalization and implementation dates for U.S. rules remain uncertain, while EU and UK rules have been finalized with phased implementation through 2027 and transitional arrangements until 2030-2032.
comparisons.comparison: Both JPM and GS are explicitly subject to U.S. federal capital and liquidity requirements that are consistent with or based on the Basel III framework. However, JPM explicitly notes that the Federal Reserve and OCC establish these requirements, while GS specifies that it and GS Bank USA are subject to 'Category I' standards due to its designation as a global systemically important bank (G-SIB).

sentences.text: We and GS Bank USA are subject to risk-based regulatory capital and leverage requirements that are calculated in accordance with the regulations of the FRB (Capital Framework).

The Capital Framework is largely based on the Basel Committee's framework for strengthening the regulation, supervision and risk management of banks (Basel III) and also implements certain provisions of the Dodd-Frank Act.

Under the U.S. federal bank regulatory agencies' tailoring framework, we and GS Bank USA are subject to "Category I" standards because we have been designated as a global systemically important bank (G-SIB).

The Federal Reserve establishes capital, liquidity and leverage requirements for JPMorganChase that are generally consistent with the international Basel III capital and liquidity framework and evaluates the Firm's compliance with those requirements.
The proposal would significantly revise risk-based capital requirements for banks with assets of $100 billion or more, including the Firm and other U.S. global systemically important banks ("GSIBs").

comparisons.peer_topic: Regulatory Oversight, Activity Limits, and Prudential Standards
comparisons.peer_summary: Morgan Stanley operates as a bank holding company and financial holding company subject to comprehensive consolidated supervision by the Federal Reserve, with the CFPB overseeing consumer protection. The BHC Act limits permitted activities, requiring Fed approval for certain actions and providing a grandfather exemption for commodities trading, while the Volcker Rule prohibits proprietary trading and certain fund investments. Capital requirements are established by the Fed and OCC based on Basel III standards, with proposed comprehensive revisions pending. The firm is subject to capital planning, stress tests, and potential dividend restrictions. Liquidity standards include the LCR and NSFR, and as a G-SIB, the firm faces single-counterparty credit limits and additional prudential standards such as limits on short-term debt and early remediation frameworks.
comparisons.comparison: Like GS, Morgan Stanley is subject to capital requirements established by the Federal Reserve that are largely based on Basel III standards. A key difference is that the target disclosure for GS specifically highlights its 'Category I' status under the tailoring framework due to its G-SIB designation, whereas the Morgan Stanley disclosure focuses more broadly on comprehensive consolidated supervision and the existence of proposed revisions to capital requirements based on Basel III without explicitly stating its specific tailoring category in the cited text.

sentences.text: The Capital Framework is largely based on the Basel Committee's framework for strengthening the regulation, supervision and risk management of banks (Basel III) and also implements certain provisions of the Dodd-Frank Act.

Under the U.S. federal bank regulatory agencies' tailoring framework, we and GS Bank USA are subject to "Category I" standards because we have been designated as a global systemically important bank (G-SIB).
Under the Capital Framework, we and GS Bank USA must meet specific regulatory capital requirements that involve quantitative measures of assets, liabilities and certain off-balance sheet items.

The Federal Reserve establishes capital requirements largely based on the Basel III capital standards established by the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision ("Basel Committee"), including well-capitalized standards, for large BHCs and evaluates our compliance with such requirements.

The Federal Reserve, Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation ("FDIC") and the OCC (collectively, "U.S. banking agencies") have proposed a comprehensive set of revisions to their capital requirements based on changes to the Basel III capital standards finalized by the Basel Committee.
